title: Transactions: what ACID actually means in practice
story:
The four letters get recited as though they were one guarantee you either have or do not. In practice two of them are close to absolute, one is your responsibility rather than the database's, and one is a dial with several settings and a default nobody in the room chose.

Start with the provenance, because it is usually stated wrong. Jim Gray presented The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations at the seventh Very Large Data Bases conference in Cannes in September 1981, describing transactions in terms of atomicity — an all-or-nothing property — consistency, and durability, the survival of a committed transaction's effects after failures. The acronym itself is not his. It appears in Härder and Reuter's 1983 paper Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery in ACM Computing Surveys, which built on the earlier transaction processing work including Gray's. Gray described the properties; Härder and Reuter named them, and he received the 1998 Turing Award for seminal contributions to database and transaction processing research and technical leadership in system implementation.

Now the four, honestly.

Atomicity is mechanical and reliable. It comes from writing the intention to a durable sequential log before performing the change, so that after any crash the system knows what was meant and can complete or undo it.

Durability is also mechanical, and its weak point is not the database. It requires the log to reach storage that survives power loss before the commit is acknowledged. If the hardware reports a write complete when it has only buffered it, the guarantee is void and the database cannot tell.

Consistency is the odd one out and is frequently misunderstood. It does not mean the database keeps your data sensible. It means the database will not violate the constraints you declared. If you did not declare that a balance cannot go negative, nothing will stop it going negative — so this letter describes a mechanism for enforcing rules, not a source of rules, and the content of it is yours.

Isolation is where the real engineering is, and where the recitation does the most damage. The strongest form — transactions behaving as though they ran one after another — is expensive, because it requires either locking that blocks concurrent work or version management that must detect and resolve conflicts. So databases offer weaker levels, and each weaker level is precisely a decision to permit a specific anomaly in exchange for concurrency.

The distinction most worth holding is between the two middle levels. Under read committed, a transaction sees only committed data, but each statement takes a fresh view — so reading the same row twice within one transaction can return different values, because another transaction committed a change in between. Under repeatable read, the transaction takes one consistent view and keeps it, so a row read twice reads the same both times.

The anomaly that distinguishes them is therefore the non-repeatable read, and it matters whenever a decision depends on reading something more than once: check a balance, do some work, check it again, act on the assumption it did not move. Under the weaker level, it moved.

Two cautions. The names are standardised but the behaviours are not identical across systems — what one database calls repeatable read may provide a snapshot that also prevents anomalies the standard permits at that level, so the level name is a starting point for reading your system's documentation rather than a specification. And the default is almost always one of the weaker levels. Most applications are running at a level nobody deliberately selected, which is fine until a piece of logic depends on a guarantee that level does not provide — at which point the bug is a rare, load-dependent, unreproducible wrong answer, which is the worst kind to find.

problem.name: Isolation is a dial
problem.shape: Concurrent transactions touch the same data and the correctness of each depends on what it can see of the others.
tell: the isolation level in use is unknown or inherited
logic reads a value, does work, and re-reads it
a wrong answer appears only under load and cannot be reproduced
correctness is being argued from the four letters rather than from a level
problem.move: Name the anomaly the logic cannot tolerate, then choose the weakest level that excludes it, and check your system's documentation rather than the standard's name. Where a decision depends on reading something twice, either raise the level or take the value once.
problem.invariant: Each isolation level below the strongest permits a specific, named anomaly in exchange for concurrency. The letters describe what the database enforces, not what your data means.
problem.breaks: The level names are standardised and the behaviours are not. What one system calls repeatable read may prevent anomalies the standard allows at that level, so reasoning from the name rather than the implementation produces a correctness argument that is right about the specification and wrong about the database.

cost.time: the strongest level blocks concurrent work or aborts transactions on conflict, so throughput falls as contention rises
cost.space: version management retains old row versions until no transaction can see them, which is work that can fall behind
cost.beats: the weakest levels, which are fast and permit anomalies most people cannot name, and taking application-level locks, which is explicit and moves a database problem into code that has no way to enforce it

worked.problem: What is the difference between read committed and repeatable read, and what anomaly does the stronger one prevent?
worked.reasoning:
Both guarantee that a transaction sees only committed data, so neither permits reading another transaction's uncommitted work. They differ in whether that view is fixed for the transaction's lifetime.

Under read committed, each statement takes a fresh view of committed data. So a row read at the start of a transaction and again later can come back different, because another transaction committed a change in between. Under repeatable read, the transaction establishes one consistent view and keeps it, so the same row read twice returns the same value both times.

The anomaly the stronger level prevents is therefore the non-repeatable read, and the reason it matters is that a great deal of ordinary logic reads something more than once without anyone noticing it has. Check a balance, perform some work, check the balance again and act on the assumption it has not moved. Under read committed it may have moved, and the decision is made on a premise that stopped being true partway through.

The failure mode is worth describing because it determines how you find it. It requires two transactions to interleave in a specific way, so it appears only under concurrency, intermittently, and usually as a wrong answer rather than an error. That is the hardest category of bug to locate — no stack trace, not reproducible on demand, and often first noticed as a discrepancy in data long after the event.

Two cautions I would attach. First, the level names are standardised and the behaviours are not identical across systems: what one database calls repeatable read may give a snapshot that also prevents anomalies the standard permits at that level. So the name is where you start reading your system's documentation, not a specification you can reason from. Second, the default is almost always one of the weaker levels, which means most applications run at a level nobody chose deliberately — fine until a piece of logic depends on a guarantee it does not provide.

It is also worth being clear about which of the four letters this is, because the recitation flattens them. Atomicity and durability are mechanical and close to absolute, resting on writing the intention to a durable log before acting. Consistency is not the database keeping your data sensible — it is the database not violating constraints you declared, so its content is yours. Isolation is the only one that is a dial, and every setting below the strongest is a deliberate exchange of a named anomaly for concurrency.

The honest summary is that the strongest level is expensive for a real reason — it needs locking that blocks work or version management that detects and resolves conflicts — so weaker levels are legitimate engineering rather than corner-cutting. The mistake is not using them. The mistake is using them without naming the anomaly you have accepted.

problem.practice: Find your database's default isolation level, then find one place in your code that reads a value, does work, and reads it again. Decide whether that logic is correct at the level you are actually running.

beats.broke: The four properties are recited as one guarantee, when two are mechanical, one is a mechanism for enforcing rules you did not supply, and one is a dial nobody set.
beats.fix: Treat isolation as the dial it is: name the anomaly the logic cannot tolerate and choose the weakest level that excludes it, checking your system's behaviour rather than the standard's name.
beats.cost: The strongest level requires locking that blocks work or version management that resolves conflicts, so every weaker level is a deliberate exchange of a named anomaly for concurrency.

interview.q: What is the difference between read committed and repeatable read, and what anomaly does the stronger one prevent?
interview.trap: Reasoning from the standard's names. Behaviours differ across systems — a database's repeatable read may prevent anomalies the standard permits at that level — so an argument from the name can be right about the specification and wrong about the database.
interview.answer:
Both guarantee a transaction sees only committed data; they differ in whether that view is fixed for the transaction's lifetime.

Under read committed each statement takes a fresh view, so a row read at the start and again later can come back different, because another transaction committed a change in between. Under repeatable read the transaction establishes one consistent view and keeps it, so the same row reads the same both times.

The anomaly the stronger level prevents is the non-repeatable read, and it matters because a great deal of ordinary logic reads something twice without anyone noticing: check a balance, do some work, check it again and act on the assumption it has not moved. Under read committed it may have moved, and the decision rests on a premise that stopped being true partway through.

The failure mode determines how you find it — it needs two transactions to interleave in a particular way, so it appears only under concurrency, intermittently, and usually as a wrong answer rather than an error. No stack trace, not reproducible on demand, often first seen as a data discrepancy long afterwards.

Two cautions. The level names are standardised and the behaviours are not, so the name is where you start reading your system's documentation rather than something to reason from. And the default is almost always a weaker level, so most applications run at one nobody chose.

It is worth placing this among the four, because the recitation flattens them: atomicity and durability are mechanical and near-absolute, resting on writing the intention to a durable log before acting; consistency is not the database keeping data sensible but the database not violating constraints you declared, so its content is yours; and isolation is the only dial.

The strongest level is expensive for a real reason, so weaker levels are legitimate engineering rather than corner-cutting. The mistake is not using them — it is using them without naming the anomaly you accepted.
